newsitem.title: GREECE: Better Greek-Turkish ties hinge on political will.
newsitem.headline: Better Greek-Turkish ties hinge on political will.

text.p: Nudged by their U.S. allies, bitter rivals Greece and Turkey set out this month to improve testy relations, ignoring domestic dissent that could trip up their efforts.

Only 18 months after the two NATO members almost went to war over a deserted Aegean islet, Greece and Turkey signed a watershed agreement in Madrid this month which could signal the start of a new stability on the military pact's eastern Mediterranean wing.
"Within this framework, Greece can now talk to Turkey directly," Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos told an Athens daily on Monday. "And this is a major political development."
Athens had in the past turned down repeated calls from Ankara to begin dialogue on all contentious issues, saying this would mean it was prepared to negotiate its sovereignty.

But the new rapprochement could falter if the governments in Athens and Ankara fail to quell internal political opposition and neglect to take further steps on the path to normal relations, political analysts said.

"It was certainly a positive move, although a bit ambiguous, I think intentionally on both sides to help them politically at home," a Western diplomat told Reuters. "It's a matter of opening communications rather than resolving issues."
The U.S.-brokered "convergence of views" signed at the NATO summit in Madrid on July 8 committed Greece and Turkey to respect each other's rights and renounce use of force.
The document avoided mention of specific problems, such as territorial waters in the Aegean, minority rights in both countries, and the divided island of Cyprus.
But it still came as a major surprise after years of vicious bickering. Greece, which waged a war of independence against the Ottoman Turks in the 1820s, sees Turkey as its main national threat.
Athens hailed the Madrid agreement as the start of a new era in Greek-Turkish affairs, saying that although no problem had been resolved, the climate now allowed direct contact.

Despite efforts to resolve disputes in recent decades, Greece and Turkey have remained bitterly opposed and have came to the brink of war, most recently in January 1996 over a deserted island known in Greek as Imia and in Turkish as Kardak.
A clash was averted after last-minute U.S. intervention and Washington has since tried to get its two bickering allies to start resolving their disputes.

Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis, eager to end festering external problems and focus on Greece's much-needed economic reforms to achieve convergence with the European Union, has appeared determined to fight off reaction from within his socialist party over the agreement.

"It appears Simitis has gained enough control over his party to push this," the western diplomat said. "It's going to benefit Greece, which will not have to over-arm to fend off danger from the east but focus on the economy instead."

But the ruling socialists have not specified the next steps towards rapprochement, apparently hesitant to make too drastic a change in their line on Turkey after decades of nationalist rhetoric by the party's late founder Andreas Papandreou.

Greek diplomats said EU-member Greece would continue to block European Union funding to Turkey until it made concrete progress on specific issues, such as taking territorial disputes to the International Court of Justice in The Hague.

"The government believed that reaction from within could be managed," a senior Greek diplomat told Reuters. "Besides, nothing was given away. We must wait and see how Turkey will apply this agreement."
A respite in Turkey's political instability, with secularists now in power after a shaky Islamist-led coalition government, would also favour the agreement, he said.
Turkey's Islamist former prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, resigned last month under pressure from the secularist army and was replaced by the secularist Mesut Yilmaz.
With secularists eager to be part of the European family, relations with Greece are bound to benefit, the Greek diplomat added.

"Turkey wants improved relations with Greece because they want to demostrate they are European material," the Western diplomat said. "Political instability could derail the effort but the will is there to pursue this no matter who is in power."
An improvement in Greek-Turkish relations is also bound to help a settlement of the Cyprus problem. U.N. efforts to reunite the island in a federation have been unsuccessful so far.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey took over the north of the island in 1974 after a coup in Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.
